text:
I can't say you're right. Your argument rests on an assumption that may not hold, and the asymmetry favors your cofounder unless a few conditions are met.

Waiting wins only if all of these are true:
- **Runway:** You'd still have at least 9-12 months of cash after the 6-month wait. A raise takes 3-6 months, so if you'd be raising on fumes, you lose negotiating leverage and risk not closing at all.
- **Metrics:** The improvement is largely within your control, not a hope. Flat or slipping metrics at month 6 means a lower valuation than today's, plus lost time.
- **Market:** Investor appetite for your category stays at least as good as now. You can't forecast that, so the wait carries risk you don't control.

The strongest case against waiting: a bad outcome from waiting (failed raise, down round, forced bridge) is far worse than a bad outcome from raising now (some extra dilution). Also, a lower valuation isn't a loss if the extra capital lets you hit those metrics faster. What matters is your ownership and odds of success at the next milestone, not the headline valuation. A high valuation you can't grow into sets up a down round later.

Your position also has a point: if the extra dilution is large and you're confident about the metrics, taking a smaller raise now (or a bridge or extension) may beat both options.

What would change my read: the current runway, how much dilution the "big round" implies versus the later raise, and how confident you are in the metric trajectory. If you can share those numbers, I can give a firmer answer.
